title: Four more mistakes and a lot more learning
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Prompted by a LinkedIn post that picked up his earlier piece on mistakes, Skelton shares four more errors from his career, three as a consultant and one working with Boards. As a consultant he failed to grasp each school's context, leaned too far toward theory rather than practical next steps, and expected change faster than busy schools could deliver. With investor-minded Board members he struggled to tell a learning story that mattered to non-educators. Each mistake comes with what he learned: start from the other party's context, pair theory with doable action, allow time for unsticking, and tell a true story that resonates. He concludes that mistakes are inevitable invitations to learn, and that beginners need the most support.
points: Consultants and new colleagues must begin from the context of the people they work with rather than offering their own past experience as the model.
Professional development must balance theory with the practical answer to what do we do, anchored in an achievable action.
Change is slow because well-practised habits must be unstuck, and the unseen messy life of a school continually intervenes.
Leaders must tell stakeholders such as non-educator Board members a true story about learning that matters to them.
Schools should not rely on lucky encounters with a mentor, but build deliberate systems that focus teachers on learning.
quotes: It can’t be that schools, other organisations and classrooms become learning-focused only if the pin-ball is lucky enough to bounce against the right stimulators. It has to be more systemic, more thought-through and more deliberate than that.

I learned that whatever I had done in the past didn’t matter if I couldn’t appreciate the context of the people I was working with now. I learned that making their context - and not mine - the frame for my work was the most essential thing I could do.

Teaching is, in the end, a practical activity that is founded, hopefully, on evidence. But whether we have evidence or not (see the early experiences of me and Diana), teachers in the classroom still have to do something every moment of every day.

I learned - again - that change is slow. I learned that it’s slow because people have to make unsticky things that had become very sticky for them over long periods of time. I learned that we have to allow time for unsticking to happen.

By the time the second part of my career started I had developed an effective story about the importance of learning and how focusing on it made the lives of teachers, school leaders and others more rewarding, less stressful and more successful. But this story didn’t really work with the money people on the Boards of my larger organisations.

Almost all of my mistakes happened at the beginning of different moments of my career. That’s why ‘Beginning’ learning is where most support is needed, with children, students, teachers, parents and other stakeholders. Getting things right at the beginning is harder to do than at any other time but more important.
We should stop treating most mistakes as a problem. Mistakes are the invitation to learn better.
